title: From a Single Crisis Line to 100,000 Lives: Chicago's Apna Ghar Turns 35
excerpt: The South Asian-founded domestic violence shelter has grown into one of America's most respected immigrant-serving organisations — and just launched a survivor-written cookbook to prove healing can happen at the kitchen table
body:
Thirty-five years ago, a group of South Asian women in Chicago picked up a phone and started answering calls from women who had nowhere else to turn. There was no building, no funding pipeline, no institutional backing — just a crisis line and the conviction that immigrant survivors of domestic violence deserved help in languages they actually spoke.

Today, Apna Ghar — Hindi for "our home" — has served over 100,000 community members from more than 50 countries, with a staff fluent in over 20 languages. The organisation operates emergency and transitional housing, runs legal and medical advocacy programmes, and provides economic empowerment services. On May 16, more than 300 of Chicago's civic, community and corporate leaders gathered at the organisation's gala, "Together We Thrive," to mark the milestone.

## 'An Incredible Foundation'

"Thirty-five years gives Apna Ghar an incredible foundation in our mission of ending gender violence," said Neha Gill, the organisation's Executive Director and CEO. "We remain determined to empower survivors, engage communities, and elevate gender justice and human rights through our evidence-based, solutions-focused approach."

The gala, hosted by Emmy Award-winning news anchor Ravi Baichwal and Rahul Sharma — founder of Strategic Inclusion Consulting and bandleader of Funkadesi — honoured individuals who have shaped Apna Ghar's trajectory.

Illinois Supreme Court Justice Sanjay T. Tailor, the first Asian American to serve on the state's highest court, received the Trailblazer Award. The Parvin and Ramzan Dhanji Foundation, longtime financial supporters, received the Champion Award. Dr. Sonia Ooyola, founder of the Be Alright Foundation, and Chef Uzma Sharif, founder of Chocolat Uzma, both received Advocacy Awards for their contributions to expanding the organisation's reach.

## Recipes from Our Home

Perhaps the most affecting milestone is the forthcoming cookbook, *Recipes from Our Home*, a collection of 29 dishes contributed by survivors who have participated in Apna Ghar's programmes.

"We've found cooking has provided its own form of common language to connect survivors with each other, creating a unique space for healing," Gill said. "This cookbook represents the bonds built through that shared comfort of eating a meal cooked with love and care."

The cookbook is dedicated to all survivors of domestic violence and celebrates the perseverance and cultures of the communities Apna Ghar serves. For an organisation that began in living rooms and community centres, a book that centres the kitchen table feels like a deliberate statement about where real healing happens.

## A Model That Other Cities Are Watching

Apna Ghar's evolution from a South Asian crisis line to a multi-ethnic, multilingual service provider has made it a model for immigrant-serving organisations across the United States. The organisation has received the Chicago Foundation for Women's award and the Chicago Mayor's Medal of Honor for exemplary service.

The model addresses a gap that mainstream domestic violence services often miss. Immigrant survivors face barriers that go beyond physical safety: language isolation, immigration status weaponised by abusive partners, cultural stigma around divorce and family separation, and a legal system that is difficult to navigate even for native English speakers. Apna Ghar's approach — culturally competent, multilingual and embedded in the communities it serves — has become a template for how to do this work properly.

## Why It Matters Beyond Chicago

For the broader Indian and South Asian diaspora in the United States, Apna Ghar's anniversary is both a celebration and a reminder. Domestic violence affects every community regardless of education, income or immigration status, but the particular vulnerabilities of immigrant women — visa dependency, family pressure, lack of independent financial resources — make organisations like Apna Ghar indispensable.

The fact that the organisation has served people from 50 countries underscores a truth that its founders understood from the beginning: the need transcends any single ethnicity or nationality. What started as a South Asian crisis line became something bigger because the problem it addressed was never limited to one community.

As Apna Ghar enters its 36th year, its trajectory offers a lesson that extends well beyond domestic violence services: the most durable institutions are often built not by policy papers or strategic plans, but by people who simply answered the phone when nobody else would.
